QID270_TEXT:
Wow, this is going to feel harsh for $7, because MOST people do not live up to their ideals. I can say I am better than I was before. Since making a big life change a couple years ago (I retired), I am eating better, sleeping better, stress is reduced, I am exercising more and I am keeping up with medical appointments. I began volunteering with an organization that raises guide dog puppies, so that hits supporting causes, community engagement, and to some extent, building relationships. But I am not working a paid job though I am still young enough that I could be, and I have some guilt about that. On the relationships axis, I am finally able to make time to work on friendships and family relationships. I've visited my elderly father twice since retiring and I'm touching base with friends more often. But again, could be doing more. On the legacy axis, I have gotten my finances cleaned up and I am making repairs and upgrades on my house, which had been deferred over the busier years. But I still need to work on an estate plan and I need to make a second go at cleaning out my junk so that the person who gets here at the end doesn't have a giant mess. 

I do spend far too much time on the internet and watching TV. I am disappointed in myself for that. But I'm a bit afraid to spend my nest egg, given how unsettled everything is. I know that time's a-wasting and there will come a time when I physically can't do these things. But's it's scary to start spending down that nest egg, give that we in the USA don't take care of our sick and elderly.

So yeah, I am still a work in progress.

QID268_TEXT: I aspire to be my old self. Back before one catastrophic illness after another ruined my life. And I do mean RUINED; from the career I loved to being near death multiple times, with hospitalizations as long as 6 months at a time. I want to be the old, active, happy, bright, cheerful 'girl' I used to be, the one who couldn't wait for morning to come, so I could see what this amazing, glorious, awesome world would bring me that day.
QID269_TEXT: I had always been a workaholic, practically from birth. I couldn't stand sitting around doing nothing, or doing nothing important. Besides working my ass off professionally, I volunteered thousands of hours and felt great about it. I wasn't doing it for a pat on the back, or to store karma for future use; I did it because it was--and is--a calling, but here I am, stuck in bed...again. I ought to still be working in my stress-filled, ultra-responsible, hugely complex job--which I LOVED. (I was the programmer, sysadmin, and manager at a major data processing company.) I ought to be the 'California girl' I once was, cherishing every moment at the beach, standing on the shore, water waving up and down my legs, absolutely in awe of how vast the Pacific really is. I ought to be back in a ballet studio, working my ass off on perfecting my technique [which is impossible--you can never reach perfection in ballet, but you keep trying]. I should be actively involved in animal rights, helping to rescue and find loving, forever homes for animals. I should be spending time with my two grandchildren--who live thousands of miles away, and since I can no longer travel, and it's hard for my daughter to coordinate trips here, we almost never see each other.
QID270_TEXT: A sad, depressed, lonely, sick person. There was one 'thing' in my life that brought me joy every single day I had her, for over 18 years: my favorite cat. She was literally ON my body 24/7 [except for eating, drinking, pottying or when I was showering]. There was something magical and mysterious about her from the very beginning, and I memorialized those beliefs in real time; they're not something I dreamed up later. We were in year 5 of renal failure when, suddenly and unexpectedly, we got up on Saturday morning and I KNEW [from her behavior] that she was going to die that day. Rather than have her least favorite person on earth [our vet] come to euthanize her, I chose to hold her, cradle her in my arms and on my heart until she died. I spent the last 5 hours of her life stroking her, kissing her, telling her what a joy she had been, not just for me, but for several other people, and how every single time I saw her, like when she re-entered the bedroom from having pottied, I'd smile. Even giggle. There was just something about her that was SO special, I can't describe it in words. Between my current catastrophic illness [Guillain-Barre Syndrome], which has left me bed-bound, and still heavily mourning the death of my cat, I'm just a miserable, unhappy, lonely person. This is NOT how I thought my life would go--I planned on working well into my 70s, not for the money [I own my 7-figure home outright] but because I loved my profession. I didn't see ANY of this coming...
